summary: Specifies a profile of ISO CLNP for use with TCP and UDP over bigger addresses as described in RFC 1347, giving the lower-layer service they expect. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: TCP and UDP want a delivery service underneath. This memo shows how to use an international one with bigger addresses.

questions: how does tcp work over clnp
subtitle: How to use ISO CLNP as the network layer for TCP and UDP with larger addresses.

tldr.problem: IP addresses are fixed at 32 bits, a limitation that will eventually run out. TCP and UDP depend on IP's datagram service to function. A larger address space is needed while maintaining TCP and UDP compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1561 specifies a profile of ISO CLNP that provides the same service as IP but with variable-length addresses up to 20 octets. It maps IP protocol fields into CLNP headers and defines how to compose pseudo-headers for TCP/UDP checksums over CLNP.
tldr.outcome: TCP and UDP can function over CLNP, enabling larger addresses in research and experimental networks. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 1561 is Experimental and served as a technical foundation for TUBA research. Ultimately, TUBA was superseded by IPv6, which also addresses the 32-bit address limitation while maintaining better compatibility with existing IP infrastructure. CLNP saw adoption in OSI networks but never became dominant in the Internet.

sections.title: CLNP as an Alternative Network Layer
sections.content: TUBA (TCP/UDP over Bigger Addresses) is a proposal to address the limitation of 32-bit IP addresses by using a different network layer protocol. The RFC assumes readers are familiar with IP (RFC 791), TCP (RFC 793), and UDP (RFC 768). It provides a mapping between CLNP, an ISO standard datagram protocol, and the expectations of TCP and UDP. Unlike IP, CLNP uses variable-length addresses of 8 to 20 octets, organized according to OSI standards. While CLNP and IP serve essentially the same role, they differ in header format, addressing, options encoding, and error reporting, so a careful mapping is required to preserve TCP and UDP semantics.
sections.eli5: IP has addresses that are always 32 bits, but CLNP uses flexible-length addresses. This RFC shows how to use CLNP underneath TCP and UDP so they can work with bigger networks.

sections.title: How CLNP Differs from IP
sections.content: CLNP and IP are both unreliable datagram protocols, but they differ in key ways. CLNP indicates header length in octets, while IP uses 32-bit words. CLNP's lifetime (TTL) is measured in 500-millisecond units rather than seconds. CLNP offers flags for fragmentation control and error reporting suppression. Most critically, CLNP uses variable-length OSI NSAP addresses, while IP uses fixed 32-bit addresses. The two protocols also encode higher-layer protocol identification differently—CLNP places a protocol selector in the address itself, while IP has a separate protocol field. For TCP and UDP to function over CLNP, these differences must be carefully handled to maintain the semantics both protocols expect.
sections.eli5: CLNP and IP are cousins, but they do things differently. CLNP uses flexible-length addresses, different timing units, and different ways to identify the protocol running on top.

sections.title: CLNP Header Structure for TUBA
sections.content: The RFC specifies how to populate CLNP header fields for TCP/UDP. The Network Layer Protocol Identifier must be set to binary 10000001 (0x81) to indicate CLNP. The Version field is set to 1. The Lifetime field is initialized to 255, corresponding to 127.5 seconds, though this value should be thought of as a rough upper bound rather than a precise timeout. The Fragmentation Permitted flag controls whether the packet may be split; when clear, it indicates a single-fragment datagram. NSAP addresses are 8 to 20 octets long, using either ANSI or GOSIP format, with the final octet containing the protocol selector for TCP (0x06) or UDP (0x11). CLNP also supports optional fields for source routing, record route, security, quality of service, padding, and timestamps, analogous to IP options but with different encoding.
sections.eli5: The CLNP header contains similar fields to IP: addresses, a lifetime counter, flags, and checksum. The main difference is that addresses can be much longer.

sections.title: Error Reporting and Pseudo-Headers
sections.content: IP uses ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) to report errors and send control messages as data inside IP datagrams. CLNP, by contrast, uses a separate message type field in the CLNP header itself. Error Reports are generated for the same conditions as ICMP: unreachable destinations, corrupted headers, congestion, and lifetime exceeded. The RFC defines reason codes that roughly map to ICMP types and codes, with CLNP offering more granular error reporting in some cases. TCP and UDP compute a checksum over the payload plus a pseudo-header derived from the network layer. Over CLNP, the pseudo-header is more complex because addresses are variable length. It includes the destination address length indicator, the full destination address (including the protocol selector byte), the source address length indicator, the full source address, a two-octet encoding of the protocol value (0x0006 for TCP, 0x0011 for UDP), and the TCP/UDP segment length. This structure allows implementations to grab a contiguous stream of octets beginning at the destination address length indicator, simplifying the composition of the pseudo-header.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, CLNP sends back an error message like ICMP does. TCP and UDP also use the addresses in a checksum formula, which must be adapted for variable-length addresses.

sections.title: CLNP Options and Their Uses
sections.content: CLNP options are encoded as triplets of parameter code, length, and value, a format that differs from IP's option encoding. The RFC specifies how to use CLNP's native options for TUBA. The Security option carries the Basic and Extended Security options from RFC 1108, prefixed with a CLNP format code indicating the source administration. The Quality of Service option is native to CLNP and more sophisticated than IP's Type of Service, supporting flags for sequence preservation, transit delay, cost, and error probability. Source routing is supported via Complete Source Route (strict) and Partial Source Route (loose) options. Record Route works similarly to IP's record route option. Timestamp is not present in the original CLNP standard but has been proposed; the RFC reserves parameter code 0xEE for it. Padding is used to align headers to convenient boundaries.
sections.eli5: CLNP has options for security, routing, quality of service, and other needs, encoded similarly to IP options but using different codes.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content: CLNP is an unreliable datagram protocol and is subject to the same security considerations as IP. The RFC does not elaborate on threat models. It notes that methods for conveying security information recommended for IP are available in CLNP via the Security option (RFC 1108). Implementers must examine the PROTO field in the source address to determine whether to apply the security option.
sections.eli5: CLNP is unreliable like IP, so it has similar security issues. The Security option can protect sensitive traffic if needed.
